496: % ======================================================================
497: \section{Appendix: usage examples}
498: \label{app:exemplos}
499: % ======================================================================
500: 
501: Command-line recipes for the most frequent use cases, checked against version V47. Commands use \code{compass.py} as the executable name, a copy of the current simulator version (\code{compass\_simV47.py}) kept under this stable name for daily use, so the examples can be copied and pasted directly. A final backslash indicates shell line continuation.
502: 
503: \subsection*{B.1 --- Basic execution (dipolar equilibrium)}
504: 
505: Square $8\times8$ array with all defaults (steel needle with automatically computed moment and inertia, no external field):
506: \begin{verbatim}
507: python3 compass.py --N 8 --M 8 --geometry square
508: \end{verbatim}
509: Generates summary images (initial state, equilibrium, comparison, order parameter) and \code{compass\_field\_log.csv} in the current directory. For the other lattices: \code{--geometry triangular} or \code{--geometry honeycomb}.
510: 
511: \subsection*{B.2 --- GPU on and off}
512: 
513: CPU is the default (\code{--gpu 0}). With V40 optimization, the CPU already handles medium arrays in seconds; GPU is useful for large arrays:
514: \begin{verbatim}
515: # CPU (default) -- medium array
516: python3 compass.py --N 30 --M 30 --t_sim 5.0
517: 
518: # GPU (CuPy/RTX 3090) -- large array; requires cupy installed
519: python3 compass.py --N 60 --M 60 --t_sim 5.0 --gpu 1
520: \end{verbatim}
521: With \code{--gpu 1}, video encoding also uses the NVENC hardware encoder when available. If CuPy is not functional, the program warns and automatically falls back to CPU.
522: 
523: \subsection*{B.3 --- Video and figures in good resolution}
524: 
525: For arrays above $15\times15$, use \code{--dpi} 150--200. Smaller \code{--frame\_every} = smoother animation (more frames):
526: \begin{verbatim}
527: python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --t_sim 4.0 \
528:     --video demo --dpi 180 --fps 30 --frame_every 3
529: \end{verbatim}
530: The video receives automatic numbering (\code{demo0000.mp4}, \code{demo0001.mp4}, \dots). To keep individual frame PNGs after assembling the video, add \code{--keep\_frames}. For static high-resolution figures only (no video), omit \code{--video} and use \code{--dpi 200}.
531: 
532: \subsection*{B.4 --- Fast sweeps: no images, no bar}
533: 
534: In campaigns with many executions, turn off all image generation (data CSVs are kept) and the progress bar:
535: \begin{verbatim}
536: python3 compass.py --N 8 --M 8 --t_sim 1.0 \
537:     --make_images 0 --progress_bar 0
538: \end{verbatim}
539: Speedup of $\sim 3\times$ in small arrays, where rendering dominates time. For \emph{uniform}-length time series across runs (no early stops by $S{=}1.00$, rest, or equilibrium), add \code{--t\_sim\_full 1} (V42).
540: 
541: \subsection*{B.5 --- Damping control (dynamic regimes)}
542: 
543: The regime is characterized by the quality factor $Q$, printed in the header of each run along with the classification (under-/overdamped). The exact $Q$ depends on the dominant field (dipolar or external); the values below, with all other parameters at default, illustrate the three regimes:
544: \begin{verbatim}
545: # underdamped (Q >> 1): visibly oscillates before stabilizing
546: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-8 --video sub
547: 
548: # intermediate (Q ~ 1): crossover
549: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 1e-6 --video middle
550: 
551: # overdamped (Q << 1): monotonic relaxation, no oscillation
552: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --damping 5e-5 --video over
553: \end{verbatim}
554: Check the printed $Q$ in the header and adjust \code{--damping} until the desired regime is reached. \code{--damping 0} disables dissipation (perpetual oscillation).
555: 
556: \subsection*{B.6 --- Needle size and spacing}
557: 
558: The radius $R$ of the circumscribed circle defines lattice spacing ($r_{nn} = 2R$); \code{--needle\_frac} defines needle length as a fraction of $2R$; sheet thickness affects automatic inertia and moment calculations:
559: \begin{verbatim}
560: # needles with 1 cm radius, occupying half the available diameter
561: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --R 0.01 --needle_frac 0.5
562: 
563: # thinner sheet (0.2 mm): lighter needle -> oscillates faster
564: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --needle_thickness 2e-4
565: 
566: # override automatic calculations with explicit values
567: python3 compass.py --N 12 --M 12 --moment 0.05 --inertia 1e-9
568: \end{verbatim}
569: 
570: \subsection*{B.7 --- External field: the six modes}
571: 
572: One example per mode, covering the full range of \code{--field\_mode}. The amplitude is \code{--B\_ext} and the direction is \code{--phi\_ext}.
573: 
574: \medskip\noindent\textbf{(1) static} --- constant (or zero) field throughout the simulation:
575: \begin{verbatim}
576: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --B_ext 1e-3 --phi_ext 45
577: \end{verbatim}
578: 
579: \noindent\textbf{(2) hysteresis} --- five-ramp cycle ($0 \to +B_{\max} \to 0 \to -B_{\max} \to 0 \to +B_{\max}$). The video (V45) shows needles and the $M\times H$ curve traced in real time, side by side. Spacing can be \code{linear} (default) or \code{log} ($\sim$15$\times$ finer sampling in the coercivity region):
580: \begin{verbatim}
581: # linear, with dual-panel video (needles + M x H curve)
582: python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --field_mode hysteresis \
583:     --B_ext 0.002 --t_sim 10.0 --video hist --dpi 160
584: 
585: # log-symmetric spacing (fine near B=0)
586: python3 compass.py --N 20 --M 20 --field_mode hysteresis \
587:     --hyst_spacing log --hyst_log_k 5 --B_ext 0.002 --t_sim 10.0
588: \end{verbatim}
589: 
590: \noindent\textbf{(3) sine} --- sinusoidal field $B(t) = B_{\max}\sin(2\pi f t)$; \code{--t\_sim} should cover several periods:
591: \begin{verbatim}
592: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode sine \
593:     --B_ext 0.002 --field_freq 0.5 --t_sim 8.0
594: \end{verbatim}
595: 
596: \noindent\textbf{(4) pulse} --- wait \code{field\_delay}, apply for \code{t\_pulse}, set to zero, and stabilize (equilibrium by $\omega$ and torque). If \code{--t\_pulse} is omitted, the legacy criterion is used (field until $S \geq 0.99$ or plateau):
597: \begin{verbatim}
598: # timed: wait 0.2 s -> field 0.3 s -> zero and stabilize
599: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode pulse \
600:     --field_delay 0.2 --t_pulse 0.3 --B_ext 0.005 --t_sim 6.0
601: 
602: # legacy (without t_pulse): field until saturation, then relaxation
603: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode pulse \
604:     --B_ext 0.005 --t_sim 6.0
605: \end{verbatim}
606: 
607: \noindent\textbf{(5) step\_pos} --- $B{=}0$ for \code{field\_delay}, then field switched on and held until the end:
608: \begin{verbatim}
609: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode step_pos \
610:     --field_delay 0.3 --B_ext 0.003 --t_sim 3.0
611: \end{verbatim}
612: 
613: \noindent\textbf{(6) step\_neg} --- field from $t{=}0$, removed at \code{field\_delay}, then kept at zero until the end:
614: \begin{verbatim}
615: python3 compass.py --N 15 --M 15 --field_mode step_neg \
616:     --field_delay 0.3 --B_ext 0.003 --t_sim 3.0
617: \end{verbatim}
618: 
619: \noindent In \code{hysteresis}, the $M(B)$ loop is exported to \code{hysteresis\_loop.csv}; in \code{sine}, to \code{sine\_field.csv}. In pulse/step modes, \code{--torque\_tol} controls the equilibrium criterion and \code{--t\_sim\_full 1} disables early stopping (Appendix~A).
620: 
621: \subsection*{B.8 --- Magnetic-domain visualization}
622: 
623: Demonstration scenario producing clear, well-separated domains (square lattice with low initial noise and long relaxation):
624: \begin{verbatim}
625: python3 compass.py --N 24 --M 24 --R 0.01 --noise 0.6 \
626:     --t_sim 8.0 --damping 3e-6 \
627:     --halo_mode domains --domain_tol 35 --video domains --dpi 160
628: \end{verbatim}
629: Each connected region of needles with similar orientation (within \code{--domain\_tol} degrees) receives a color; small domains appear in gray. Smaller tolerances, for example the default $15^\circ$, fragment more; larger tolerances aggregate more. From V43 onward, halos (domain or order) appear in \emph{all} figures: \code{compass\_initial}, \code{compass\_equilibrium}, video frames, and also \code{compass\_comparison}, whose panels show the domain count for each state in the title.
630: 
631: \subsection*{B.9 --- Periodic boundary conditions and reproducibility}
632: 
633: \begin{verbatim}
634: # array treated as an infinite periodic structure (1 replica per side)
635: python3 compass.py --N 16 --M 16 --pbc 1 --pbc_images 1
636: 
637: # exact reproducibility: fix the initial-noise seed
638: python3 compass.py --N 10 --M 10 --seed 123
639: \end{verbatim}
640: 
641: \subsection*{B.10 --- Full scientific campaign (satellite scripts)}
642: 
643: \begin{verbatim}
644: # quick environment validation (seconds)
645: python3 damping_sweepV02.py --out_dir results --quick_test 1
646: 
647: # full Study 1 campaign, parallel on 8 cores
648: python3 damping_sweepV02.py --out_dir results \
649:     --grid_n 30 --n_seeds 5 --n_dampings 8 \
650:     --Q_min 0.05 --Q_max 15.0 \
651:     --geometries square,triangular,honeycomb --n_workers 8
652: 
653: # resume interrupted campaign (skip already registered runs)
654: python3 damping_sweepV02.py --out_dir results ... --resume 1
655: 
656: # analysis: loop metrics, avalanches, tau(Q), domains
657: python3 damping_sweep_analysis.py --sweep_dir results \
658:     --out_dir analysis
659: \end{verbatim}
660: Avoid combining \code{--n\_workers} $> 1$ with \code{--use\_gpu 1}, due to GPU contention between processes.
661:

262: In an interactive terminal (TTY), ANSI codes move the cursor and clear lines so the two lines are redrawn in place instead of accumulating new lines. For redirected output (non-TTY), the function uses the legacy behavior: the bar is updated with '\r' on a single line, and the caller prints status as normal log lines.
263: 
264: Parameters
265: ----------
266: frac        : completed fraction, between 0.0 and 1.0
267: prefix      : text before the bar, e.g. "Integrating [CPU] "
268: suffix      : text after the percentage, e.g. "step 524/1007"
269: status_line : second panel line, or None
270: bar_width   : number of characters in the bar itself
271: 
272: Note: any normal _print() message emitted while the panel is open should come after _print_progress_bar_finish(), which moves the cursor below the panel and marks it as closed."""
273:     import sys
274:     frac = max(0.0, min(1.0, frac))
275:     n_filled = int(round(frac * bar_width))
276:     bar = '#' * n_filled + ' ' * (bar_width - n_filled)
277:     pct = frac * 100.0
278:     bar_line = f"{prefix}[{bar}] {pct:5.1f}%  {suffix}"
279: 
280:     if _progress_ansi_ok():
281:         status = status_line if status_line is not None else ""
282:         # Protocol with cursor invariant (V44): at the END of each drawing,
283:         # the cursor remains parked at COLUMN 0 OF THE BAR LINE (top of the
284:         # panel). Each update then redraws downward:
285:         #   clear line (\x1b[K) + bar + moves down ("\n\r", robust with or
286:         #   without translation ONLCR by the terminal driver) + clears + status +
287:         #   moves up (\x1b[1THE) + returns to column 0 (\r).
288:         # This is independent of the position where the text ends (without depending
289:         # on \n returning to column 0, which varies between terminals/ptys) and
290:         # works at the bottom of the screen (the "\n" causes the required scroll).
291:         seq = ("\x1b[K" + bar_line + "\n\r" +
292:                "\x1b[K" + status + "\x1b[1A\r")
293:         sys.stdout.write(seq)
294:         sys.stdout.flush()
295:         _PROGRESS_REGION['open'] = True
296:     else:
297:         # legacy (not-TTY): bar overwriting its own line via \r
298:         sys.stdout.write("\r" + bar_line)
299:         sys.stdout.flush()
300: 
301: 
302: def _print_progress_bar_finish():
303:     """Closes the progress panel: moves the cursor to a new clean line below the panel, keeps the final two lines visible, and marks the panel as closed. In ANSI mode it is safe to call this when the panel is already closed, because it emits nothing and avoids spurious blank lines."""
304:     import sys
305:     if _progress_ansi_ok():
306:         if _PROGRESS_REGION['open']:
307:             # cursor is at column 0 of the bar line: move down two lines
308:             # (bar -> status -> new line below the panel)
309:             sys.stdout.write('\n\r\n\r')
310:             sys.stdout.flush()
311:             _PROGRESS_REGION['open'] = False
312:     else:
313:         sys.stdout.write('\r\n')
314:         sys.stdout.flush()

317: # 1. PHYSICAL CONSTANTS (International System — SI)
318: # ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
319: 
320: # μ₀/(4π) = 1×10⁻⁷  T·m/A  (vacuum permeability / 4π)
321: MU0_OVER_4PI = 1.0e-7   # T·m/A
322: 
323: # ── Default physical parameters of a table compass needle (~5 cm) ──────
324: #
325: # Magnetic moment
326: MOMENT_DEFAULT = 0.1      # A·m²   (typical table compass needle)
327: #
328: # Needle mass and geometry (thin steel bar, length L, circular cross section)
329: #   mass   m ≈ 0.5 g  = 5×10⁻⁴ kg
330: #   length L ≈ 5 cm = 0.05 m
331: #   Moment of inertia of thin bar about its center:
332: #       I = (1/12) · m · L²  =  (1/12) · 5×10⁻⁴ · (0.05)²  ≈ 1.04×10⁻⁷  kg·m²
333: INERTIA_DEFAULT = 1.0e-7  # kg·m²
334: 
335: # Density of common magnetic steel (carbon steel / silicon steel for use
336: # electromagnetic, the used in transformer laminations or compasss
337: # of mesa). Typically ranges between 7700-7900 kg/m³; we use the value
338: # representative of the ordinary carbon steel.
339: STEEL_DENSITY_DEFAULT = 7850.0   # kg/m³
340: # Default thickness of a thin sheet cut from ordinary steel sheet
341: NEEDLE_THICKNESS_DEFAULT = 0.4e-3   # m  (0.4 mm)
342: 
343: # Saturation magnetization of a common magnetic steel (carbon steel / ferro
344: # doce). Corresponds to a saturatestion flux density Bsat ≈ 2.0 T,
345: # well-established value in the literature for iron alloys of alta
346: # permeability (typical range: 1.6-2.2 T; we use the value central
347: # representative). Relation: Bsat = μ0 · Ms  →  Ms = Bsat / μ0.
348: STEEL_MS_SATURATION_DEFAULT = 1.59e6   # A/m  (≈ Bsat of 2.0 T)
349: 
350: 
351: def compute_inertia_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness,
352:                                   density=STEEL_DENSITY_DEFAULT):
353:     """Computes the moment of inertia of a needle modeled as a thin, homogeneous rectangular sheet rotating about the axis perpendicular to the sheet plane and passing through the center of mass. This is the z axis and represents the real rotation axis of a compass needle supported by a pivot.
354: 
355: Physical model
356: --------------
357: Rectangular sheet with length L, width w, thickness t, mass m, and density rho:
358: 
359:     m = rho · L · w · t                         [kg]
360: 
361: Moment of inertia of a thin rectangular plate about the axis perpendicular to its plane through the center:
362: 
363:     I = (1/12) · m · (L² + w²)                  [kg·m²]
364: 
365: This formula generalizes the thin-bar case, I = mL²/12, valid when w -> 0. Here the w² term is kept explicitly because real needles cut from sheet metal have non-negligible width. The thickness t enters only through the mass. A thin sheet has a negligible intrinsic inertia term in the direction perpendicular to its plane, m·t²/12, when t << L,w.
366: 
367: Parameters
368: ----------
369: needle_len   : needle length L [m]
370: needle_width : needle width w [m]
371: thickness    : sheet thickness t [m]
372: density      : material density [kg/m³], default: common magnetic steel, 7850 kg/m³
373: 
374: Returns
375: -------
376: I : moment of inertia [kg·m²]"""
377:     mass = density * needle_len * needle_width * thickness   # [kg]
378:     I = (1.0 / 12.0) * mass * (needle_len**2 + needle_width**2)   # [kg·m²]
379:     return I
380: 
381: 
382: def compute_moment_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness,
383:                                  Ms=STEEL_MS_SATURATION_DEFAULT):
384:     """Computes the magnetic moment of a needle modeled as a thin rectangular sheet of magnetic steel, saturated along its long axis, the north direction of the needle. In other words, the whole needle is assumed to be magnetized up to the material's physical limit, with all magnetic domains aligned along its length.
385: 
386: Physical model
387: --------------
388: For a saturated ferromagnetic material, the total magnetic moment is the product of saturation magnetization Ms and volume V:
389: 
390:     m = Ms · V                                  [A·m²]
391:     V = L · w · t                               [m³]
392: 
393: This is the same rectangular-sheet geometry L×w×t used in the inertia calculation. Here the full needle volume is assumed to contribute to magnetization, an ideal case of uniform saturation. Real needles may have magnetization slightly below the theoretical saturation because of shape demagnetization, but full saturation is the physical upper limit and a reasonable reference for a well-magnetized needle.
394: 
395: Parameters
396: ----------
397: needle_len   : needle length L [m]
398: needle_width : needle width w [m]
399: thickness    : sheet thickness t [m]
400: Ms           : material saturation magnetization [A/m], default: common magnetic steel, about 1.59e6 A/m, corresponding to Bsat ≈ 2.0 T
401: 
402: Returns
403: -------
404: m : magnetic moment [A·m²]"""
405:     volume = needle_len * needle_width * thickness   # [m³]
406:     m = Ms * volume                                   # [A·m²]
407:     return m
408: 
409: #
410: # Viscous damping (air resistance to needle rotation).
411: # The effective Q depends of the dominant field B_eff = max(B_dipolar, B_externo):
412: #   Q = omega_0·I/b   where  omega_0 = sqrt(m·B_eff/I)
413: #
414: # With B_ext = 0.1 T:   omega_0 ≈ 316 rad/s  →  b = 8and-6 gives Q ≈ 4  (smooth)
415: # With B_ext = 0  :     omega_0 ≈  13 rad/s  →  b = 5and-8 gives Q ≈ 25 (compass)
416: #
417: # The default 5e-8 is suitable for simulating with no external field or weak field.
418: # For strong fields (> 1 mT), use --damping 1and-6 the 1and-5 for smooth motion.
419: DAMPING_DEFAULT = 5.0e-8  # N·m·s/rad
420:

423: # 2. MAGNETIC DIPOLAR FIELD (SI)
424: # ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
425: 
426: def dipole_field_2d(rx, ry, theta_src, moment):
427:     """Computes the magnetic field produced by a dipole in the XY plane, using SI units.
428: 
429: Exact 3D magnetic-dipole field, evaluated in the z=0 plane:
430: 
431:     B = (mu0/4pi) · [ 3(m_hat·r_hat)r_hat - m_hat ] / r³
432: 
433: In Cartesian components, with m = moment·(cos theta, sin theta, 0):
434: 
435:     Bx = (mu0/4pi) · [ 3(m·r)·rx / r⁵ - mx / r³ ]
436:     By = (mu0/4pi) · [ 3(m·r)·ry / r⁵ - my / r³ ]
437: 
438: SI units:
439:     moment [A·m²]
440:     rx, ry [m]
441:     Bx, By [T]
442: 
443: Parameters
444: ----------
445: rx, ry    : components of r = receiver point - source dipole [m]
446: theta_src : angle of the source dipole relative to the +x axis [rad]
447: moment    : magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment of the source needle [A·m²]
448: 
449: Returns
450: -------
451: (Bx, By) : magnetic-field components at (rx, ry) [T]"""
452:     r2 = rx**2 + ry**2
453:     if r2 < 1e-24:
454:         # avoids division by zero when the point coincides with the source
455:         return 0.0, 0.0
456: 
457:     r  = np.sqrt(r2)          # distance  [m]
458:     r5 = r2 * r2 * r          # r⁵  [m⁵]
459: 
460:     mx = moment * np.cos(theta_src)   # x component of the moment  [THE·m²]
461:     my = moment * np.sin(theta_src)   # y component of the moment  [THE·m²]
462: 
463:     mdotr = mx * rx + my * ry         # m · r  [THE·m³]
464: 
465:     Bx = MU0_OVER_4PI * (3.0 * mdotr * rx / r5  -  mx / (r2 * r))
466:     By = MU0_OVER_4PI * (3.0 * mdotr * ry / r5  -  my / (r2 * r))
467:     return Bx, By   # [T]
468: 
469:

471: # 3. TOTAL FIELD ON THE NEEDLE (SI)
472: # ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
473: 
474: def total_field_on(i, j, thetas, xs, ys, cutoff, moment,
475:                    pbc=False, Lx=None, Ly=None, n_images=1):
476:     """Sums the dipolar field from all neighboring needles onto needle (i, j).
477: 
478: For computational efficiency, only needles within the cutoff radius are considered. This is physically justified because the dipolar field decays as 1/r³, so distant contributions are negligible.
479: 
480: Periodic boundary conditions (PBC)
481: ----------------------------------
482: When pbc=True, the lattice is treated as a unit cell repeated infinitely in x and y, creating a periodic structure without edges. For each needle pair (i,j)-(ni,nj), the field is summed over all periodic replicas within ±n_images cells in x and y, not only the nearest image. With n_images=1, the default, each neighbor contributes through (2·1+1)² = 9 replicas: the original cell plus one replica on each side in x and y, equivalent to the classical minimum-image convention. Increasing n_images includes more distant replicas and is useful when the cutoff is large relative to the lattice period.
483: 
484: This removes edge effects: needles at the boundary see neighbors from the opposite side, and their more distant replicas, as if the structure were infinite.
485: 
486: Parameters
487: ----------
488: i, j     : indices of the receiver needle in the N×M grid
489: thetas   : 2D array with current angles of all needles [rad]
490: xs, ys   : 2D arrays with fixed needle positions [m]
491: cutoff   : maximum interaction radius [m]
492: moment   : magnetic moment of each needle [A·m²]
493: pbc      : if True, applies periodic boundary conditions [bool]
494: Lx, Ly   : lattice periods in x and y [m], required only when pbc=True and computed in make_grid
495: n_images : number of periodic replicas to sum on each side in each direction, default 1. Total replicas considered per neighbor = (2·n_images+1)² cells.
496: 
497: Returns
498: -------
499: (Bx_tot, By_tot) : total field at needle (i, j) [T]"""
500:     Bx_tot, By_tot = 0.0, 0.0
501:     N, M = thetas.shape
502:     xi, yi = xs[i, j], ys[i, j]
503: 
504:     # periodic replica shifts to consider (0 = original cell)
505:     if pbc and Lx and Ly:
506:         img_range = range(-n_images, n_images + 1)
507:         x_shifts = [k * Lx for k in img_range]
508:         y_shifts = [k * Ly for k in img_range]
509:     else:
510:         x_shifts = [0.0]
511:         y_shifts = [0.0]
512: 
513:     for ni in range(N):
514:         for nj in range(M):
515:             if ni == i and nj == j and not pbc:
516:                 continue  # without PBC: the needle does not interact with itself
517: 
518:             rx0 = xi - xs[ni, nj]   # [m]
519:             ry0 = yi - ys[ni, nj]   # [m]
520: 
521:             for dx_img in x_shifts:
522:                 for dy_img in y_shifts:
523:                     # skips the needle itself in the original cell (zero distance)
524:                     if ni == i and nj == j and dx_img == 0.0 and dy_img == 0.0:
525:                         continue
526: 
527:                     rx = rx0 + dx_img
528:                     ry = ry0 + dy_img
529:                     dist = np.sqrt(rx*rx + ry*ry)
530: 
531:                     if dist > cutoff:
532:                         continue  # outside the cutoff radius: ignore
533: 
534:                     bx, by = dipole_field_2d(rx, ry, thetas[ni, nj], moment)
535:                     Bx_tot += bx
536:                     By_tot += by
537: 
538:     return Bx_tot, By_tot   # [T]
539:

653: # 3b. VECTORIZED CALCULATION OF THE DIPOLAR FIELD AND TORQUES (GPU/CPU)
654: # ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
655: 
656: def compute_torques_vectorized(theta_flat, x_flat, y_flat, moment, cutoff,
657:                                bx_ext, by_ext,
658:                                pbc=False, Lx=None, Ly=None, n_images=1):
659:     """Computes the magnetic torque on each needle by summing the dipolar field from all other needles, fully vectorized without Python loops.
660: 
661: This function replaces the double loop `for i: for j: total_field_on(...)` with array operations (broadcasting), which makes it possible to run on the GPU through CuPy, whose syntax is identical to NumPy, when available, or normally on the CPU through NumPy. The complexity remains O(K²), where K = N×M, because every needle interacts with every other needle, but the sum is performed in parallel over all GPU/CPU cores at once instead of sequentially in Python. Typical speedups on GPUs such as the RTX 3090 are 10-100x for large lattices (K > about 400 needles).
662: 
663: Physics, identical to total_field_on/dipole_field_2d but vectorized:
664: 
665:     B = (mu0/4pi) · [ 3(m_hat·r_hat)r_hat - m_hat ] / r³
666: 
667: Parameters
668: ----------
669: theta_flat : 1D array (K,) with all needle angles [rad]
670: x_flat, y_flat : 1D arrays (K,) with all needle positions [m]
671: moment     : magnetic moment of each needle [A·m²]
672: cutoff     : maximum interaction radius [m]
673: bx_ext, by_ext : instantaneous external-field components [T]
674: pbc        : if True, sums periodic replicas (see total_field_on)
675: Lx, Ly     : lattice periods in x and y [m], required if pbc=True
676: n_images   : number of replicas on each side in each direction (PBC)
677: 
678: Returns
679: -------
680: tau_flat : 1D array (K,) with the torque on each needle [N·m], in the same backend as theta_flat, GPU or CPU"""
681:     # detects the backend from the input array (instead of using the
682:     # module global _xp) — so the function correctly respects the
683:     # effective backend chosen by the caller (CPU or GPU via --gpu),
684:     # even if the global GPU detection is different
685:     if _GPU_AVAILABLE and hasattr(theta_flat, 'get'):
686:         xp = cp   # theta_flat is an array CuPy (GPU)
687:     else:
688:         xp = np   # theta_flat is an array NumPy (CPU)
689:     K  = theta_flat.shape[0]
690: 
691:     # magnetic-moment vectors of each source needle
692:     mx = moment * xp.cos(theta_flat)   # (K,)
693:     my = moment * xp.sin(theta_flat)   # (K,)
694: 
695:     # periodic shifts to sum (0.0 single one if pbc=False)
696:     if pbc and Lx and Ly:
697:         img_range = range(-n_images, n_images + 1)

1258:     # Ctrl+I in the terminal sends the ASCII character \t (TAB, code 9).

1262:     import threading, sys, os as _os

1264:     _stop_flag = threading.Event()   # set by the thread or by S=1

1266:     # original terminal state — saved in the outer scope for garantir

1269:     # terminal may remain in raw mode after the program exits, deixando
1270:     # the shell (zsh/bash) with broken output in subsequent commands.
1271:     _term_fd  = None
1272:     _term_old = None
1273:     try:
1274:         import termios

1280:     def _restore_terminal():
1281:         """Restores the terminal to normal cooked mode if it was changed."""
1282:         if _term_fd is not None and _term_old is not None:
1283:             try:
1284:                 import termios
1285:                 termios.tcsetattr(_term_fd, termios.TCSADRAIN, _term_old)
1286:             except Exception:
1287:                 pass

1289:     # registers as the final safety net: ensures restoration even in
1290:     # case of an unhandled exception, Ctrl+C, or any abrupt termination
1291:     import atexit
1292:     atexit.register(_restore_terminal)

1294:     def _keyboard_listener():
1295:         """Keyboard-listener thread for Ctrl+I (Tab).
1296: 
1297: Goal: allow interrupting a long simulation and immediately finishing/saving the video, instead of losing all frames already generated.
1298: 
1299: Implementation:
1300: - on POSIX systems, puts stdin in cbreak mode and reads one character at a time;
1301: - Ctrl+I and Tab have ASCII code 9, so either key sets the stop flag;
1302: - in non-interactive environments, the listener simply returns."""
1303:         try:
1304:             import tty, termios
1305:             fd = sys.stdin.fileno()
1306:             tty.setraw(fd)
1307:             while not _stop_flag.is_set():
1308:                 ch = _os.read(fd, 1)
1309:                 if ch == b'\t':          # Ctrl+I = TAB = ASCII 9
1310:                     _stop_flag.set()
1311:                     break
1312:                 elif ch == b'\x03':      # Ctrl+C = ETX = ASCII 3
1313:                     # IMMEDIATE and unconditional termination. In mode raw,
1314:                     # the terminal does not automatically generate SIGINT from
1315:                     # of Ctrl+C (this is disabled together with the rest of the
1316:                     # special processing of control characters).
1317:                     # Manually resending SIGINT (the.kill) was tested and
1318:                     # proved unreliable: when the thread main
1319:                     # is in a blocking call (e.g., waiting for this
1320:                     # same thread, or inside a long NumPy operation),
1321:                     # the signal delivery may never occur. Therefore here
1322:                     # we terminate the process directly — without waiting the
1323:                     # thread main "to notice" anything. Restauramos the
1324:                     # terminal first, since the._exit() skips any
1325:                     # finally/atexit from the rest of the program.
1326:                     _restore_terminal()
1327:                     sys.stdout.write("\r\n  Abortado (Ctrl+C) — encerramento imediato.\r\n")
1328:                     sys.stdout.flush()
1329:                     _os._exit(130)   # 130 = conventional exit code for SIGINT
1330:         except Exception:
1331:             # stdin is not the terminal (redirection, pipe, Windows without
1332:             # msvcrt) — silently disables the keyboard listening
1333:             pass
1334:         finally:
1335:             _restore_terminal()

1348:     def field_at(t):
1349:         """Computes the instantaneous signed external field for the selected field mode.
1350: 
1351: Returns (bx, by, B_scalar), where B_scalar is the signed projection along phi_ext. In static mode, the scalar is positive. In hysteresis and sine modes, it changes sign according to the ramp or sinusoid."""

1353:             return Bext_x0, Bext_y0
1354: 
1355:         elif field_mode == 'hysteresis':
1356:             # Full cycle: 0→+Bmax→0→-Bmax→0→+Bmax
1357:             # 5 segments of t5 = t_sim/5. Within each segment, u0 is the
1358:             # fraction traversed from of the endpoint B=0 of the segmento.
1359:             #
1360:             # hyst_spacing='linear' (default): |B| = Bmax·u0  (V40 and earlier)
1361:             # hyst_spacing='log'   : |B| = Bmax·sinh(k·u0)/sinh(k)
1362:             #     symmetric log-like spacing (via sinh, because the pure log
1363:             #     does not cross zero): dB/dt small near B=0 → amostragem
1364:             #     FINE field sampling in the transition/coercivity region; dB/dt
1365:             #     large near ±Bmax → COARSE sampling at saturation.
1366:             #     k (hyst_log_k) controls the concentratestion: k→0 recupera the
1367:             #     linear; k=5 concentrates ~15x more points near of B=0 of the
1368:             #     than near saturation.
1369:             T  = t_sim if t_sim > 0 else 1.0
1370:             t5 = T / 5.0
1371:             if t <= t5:                      # seg 1: 0 → +Bmax
1372:                 u0, sgn = (t / t5), +1.0
1373:             elif t <= 2.0 * t5:              # seg 2: +Bmax → 0
1374:                 u0, sgn = (1.0 - (t - t5) / t5), +1.0
1375:             elif t <= 3.0 * t5:              # seg 3: 0 → -Bmax
1376:                 u0, sgn = ((t - 2.0 * t5) / t5), -1.0
1377:             elif t <= 4.0 * t5:              # seg 4: -Bmax → 0
1378:                 u0, sgn = (1.0 - (t - 3.0 * t5) / t5), -1.0
1379:             else:                            # seg 5: 0 → +Bmax
1380:                 u0, sgn = ((t - 4.0 * t5) / t5), +1.0
1381:             if hyst_spacing == 'log' and hyst_log_k > 1e-9:
1382:                 # clamp only in log mode: the final step may fall beyond of
1383:                 # t_sim (u0 slightly > 1) and the sinh amplificaria esse
1384:                 # overshoot exponencialmente. No linear mode the overshoot
1385:                 # residual (~dt/t5 of B_max) is kept for compatibility
1386:                 # bit-for-bit with V40 and earlier.
1387:                 u0 = min(max(u0, 0.0), 1.0)
1388:                 g = np.sinh(hyst_log_k * u0) / np.sinh(hyst_log_k)
1389:             else:
1390:                 g = u0
1391:             B_scalar = sgn * B_max * g
1392:             return B_scalar * cos_phi, B_scalar * sin_phi

1935:     import subprocess, shutil, os

2004: # 5. GENERATION OF THE NEEDLE GRID
2005: # ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
2006: 
2007: def make_grid(N=8, M=8, geometry='square', noise=1.5, R=0.025):
2008:     """Creates the positions and initial angles of an N×M grid of needles.
2009: 
2010: The unifying parameter is R [m], the radius of the circle enclosing each needle. Positions are computed so adjacent circles touch tangentially, with center-to-center distance 2R, ensuring a visually correct lattice without circle overlap in any geometry.
2011: 
2012: Parameters
2013: ----------
2014: N, M      : number of needle rows and columns
2015: geometry  : lattice type
2016: noise     : random-noise amplitude in the initial angles [rad]; 0 means all needles point to +x, and pi means fully random orientation
2017: R         : radius of the circle enclosing each needle [m], default 0.025 m = 2.5 cm
2018: seed      : random-number-generator seed
2019: 
2020: Returns
2021: -------
2022: thetas    : N×M array of initial angles [rad]
2023: xs, ys    : N×M arrays of needle-center positions [m]
2024: Lx, Ly    : lattice periods for periodic boundary conditions [m]"""
2025:     s3 = np.sqrt(3.0)
2026: 
2027:     # ── grid square ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2028:     if geometry == 'square':
2029:         d = 2.0 * R          # distance between neighbors
2030:         xs = np.zeros((N, M))
2031:         ys = np.zeros((N, M))
2032:         for i in range(N):
2033:             for j in range(M):
2034:                 xs[i, j] = j * d
2035:                 ys[i, j] = i * d
2036:         thetas = noise * np.random.randn(N, M)
2037:         Lx, Ly = M * d, N * d   # period of the lattice for PBC [m]
2038:         return xs, ys, thetas, d, Lx, Ly
2039: 
2040:     # ── grid triangular equilateral ───────────────────────────────────────
2041:     elif geometry == 'triangular':
2042:         d      = 2.0 * R          # distance between neighbors
2043:         dx_col = d                # spacing between columns
2044:         dy_row = R * s3           # spacing between rows = R·√3 = d·(√3/2)
2045:         offset = R                # odd-row offset = R = d/2
2046:         xs = np.zeros((N, M))
2047:         ys = np.zeros((N, M))
2048:         for i in range(N):
2049:             x_off = offset * (i % 2)
2050:             for j in range(M):
2051:                 xs[i, j] = j * dx_col + x_off
2052:                 ys[i, j] = i * dy_row
2053:         thetas = noise * np.random.randn(N, M)
2054:         Lx, Ly = M * dx_col, N * dy_row   # period of the lattice for PBC [m]
2055:         return xs, ys, thetas, d, Lx, Ly
2056: 
2057:     # ── grid honeycomb (honeycomb) ──────────────────────────────────────────
2058:     elif geometry == 'honeycomb':
2059:         dy  = R * np.sqrt(3.0)   # spacing vertical between rows [m]
2060:         d   = 2.0 * R            # distance between neighbors [m]
2061: 
2062:         # Target rectangle dimensions
2063:         W = (M - 1) * 2.0 * R   # width: M needles in a complete row
2064:         H = (N - 1) * dy         # altura:  N rows with spacing dy
2065: 
2066:         # Generates lattice larger (padding of 2 rows/columns in each side)
2067:         N_rows = (N + 4) * 2     # * 2 porque alternamos pair and odd
2068:         x_start = -2.0 * 2 * R   # starts two needles to the left
2069:         y_start = -2.0 * dy       # starts two rows below
2070: 
2071:         xs_list, ys_list = [], []
2072:         for row in range(N_rows):
2073:             y = y_start + row * dy
2074:             if row % 2 == 0:
2075:                 # complete row: x = x_start, x_start+2R, x_start+4R, ...
2076:                 x = x_start
2077:                 while x <= W + 2 * 2 * R:
2078:                     xs_list.append(x)
2079:                     ys_list.append(y)
2080:                     x += 2.0 * R
2081:             else:
2082:                 # row meia: x = x_start+R, x_start+5R, x_start+9R, ...
2083:                 # offset of R relative to the row pair, step 4R
2084:                 x = x_start + R
2085:                 while x <= W + 2 * 2 * R:
2086:                     xs_list.append(x)
2087:                     ys_list.append(y)
2088:                     x += 4.0 * R
2089: 
2090:         all_x = np.array(xs_list)
2091:         all_y = np.array(ys_list)
2092: 
2093:         # Clip: keeps points inside the target rectangle with margin R
2094:         margin = R * 0.99
2095:         mask = ((all_x >= -margin) & (all_x <= W + margin) &
2096:                 (all_y >= -margin) & (all_y <= H + margin))
2097:         clipped_x = all_x[mask]
2098:         clipped_y = all_y[mask]
2099: 
2100:         n_pts = len(clipped_x)
2101:         xs     = clipped_x.reshape(n_pts, 1)
2102:         ys     = clipped_y.reshape(n_pts, 1)
2103:         thetas = noise * np.random.randn(n_pts, 1)
2104:         Lx, Ly = W, H   # period aproximado of the lattice for PBC [m]
2105:         return xs, ys, thetas, d, Lx, Ly
2106: 
2107:     else:
2108:         raise ValueError(f"Geometria desconhecida: '{geometry}'. "
2109:                          "Use 'square', 'triangular' ou 'honeycomb'.")
2110:

2113: # 5b. IDENTIFICATION OF MAGNETIC DOMAINS
2114: # ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
2115: 
2116: def label_magnetic_domains(thetas, tol_deg=15.0):
2117:     """Identifies magnetic domains: connected regions of neighboring needles whose angular difference remains within a tolerance tol_deg.
2118: 
2119: Unlike the local order parameter, shown as green/red halos and measuring only the average alignment of each needle with its neighbors, this function groups the whole lattice into regions. Each region receives a distinct integer label, analogous to real magnetic domains: areas where magnetization points essentially in the same direction, separated by domain walls where orientation changes abruptly beyond the tolerance.
2120: 
2121: Algorithm
2122: ---------
2123: Union-Find (disjoint-set) over the N×M grid. Direct neighbors (up/down/left/right, the same neighborhood used for the local order parameter) are merged when their angular difference modulo 2pi is <= tol_deg. The result is then relabeled compactly from 0 to n_domains-1.
2124: 
2125: Returns
2126: -------
2127: labels    : N×M integer array with domain labels
2128: n_domains : number of domains"""
2129:     N, M = thetas.shape
2130:     K = N * M
2131:     parent = np.arange(K)
2132: 
2133:     def find(x):
2134:         root = x
2135:         while parent[root] != root:
2136:             root = parent[root]
2137:         while parent[x] != root:
2138:             parent[x], x = root, parent[x]
2139:         return root
2140: 
2141:     def union(a, b):
2142:         ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
2143:         if ra != rb:
2144:             parent[ra] = rb
2145: 
2146:     tol_rad = np.deg2rad(tol_deg)
2147: 
2148:     def _angdiff(a, b):
2149:         # minimum angular difference on the circle, always in [0, π]
2150:         d = a - b
2151:         return np.abs(np.arctan2(np.sin(d), np.cos(d)))
2152: 
2153:     idx_grid = np.arange(K).reshape(N, M)
2154: 
2155:     # vertical pairs (i, i+1) whose angular difference is within the tolerance
2156:     if N > 1:
2157:         d_vert = _angdiff(thetas[:-1, :], thetas[1:, :])
2158:         mask_vert = d_vert <= tol_rad
2159:         pairs_a = [idx_grid[:-1, :][mask_vert]]
2160:         pairs_b = [idx_grid[1:, :][mask_vert]]
2161:     else:
2162:         pairs_a, pairs_b = [], []
2163: 
2164:     # pairs horizontais (j, j+1)
2165:     if M > 1:
2166:         d_horiz = _angdiff(thetas[:, :-1], thetas[:, 1:])
2167:         mask_horiz = d_horiz <= tol_rad
2168:         pairs_a.append(idx_grid[:, :-1][mask_horiz])
2169:         pairs_b.append(idx_grid[:, 1:][mask_horiz])
2170: 
2171:     if pairs_a:
2172:         flat_a = np.concatenate(pairs_a)
2173:         flat_b = np.concatenate(pairs_b)
2174:         for a, b in zip(flat_a.tolist(), flat_b.tolist()):
2175:             union(a, b)
2176: 
2177:     labels_raw = np.array([find(k) for k in range(K)])
2178:     _, labels_remapped = np.unique(labels_raw, return_inverse=True)
2179:     n_domains = int(labels_remapped.max()) + 1 if K > 0 else 0
2180:     return labels_remapped.reshape(N, M), n_domains
2181:

2183: def _domain_color_palette(n_domains):
2184:     """Generates visually distinct and deterministic colors for n_domains domains, so the same domain label maps to the same color across frames and calls. Uses matplotlib's 'hsv' colormap sampled at regular hue intervals. Works well for a few domains and remains usable for many domains until the palette becomes visually dense, which is inherent to any palette with dozens of categories.
2185: 
2186: Parameters
2187: ----------
2188: n_domains : number of domains to color
2189: 
2190: Returns
2191: -------
2192: array (n_domains, 4) with RGBA colors"""
2193:     if n_domains <= 1:
2194:         return np.array([[0.55, 0.55, 0.85, 1.0]])
2195:     hues = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_domains, endpoint=False)
2196:     # small shift (golden ratio) prevents neighboring domains in
2197:     # numeric label (which also tends to reflect spatial neighbors, since
2198:     # the union-find rotula in order of varredura) caiam in matizes nearby
2199:     hues = (hues * 0.618034 + 0.15) % 1.0
2200:     return cm.hsv(hues)

2207: def draw_compass(ax, x, y, theta, length=0.42, width=0.10,
2208:                  color_n='#FFFFFF', color_s='#2E6DB4',
2209:                  edge='#1a1a1a', zorder=4):
2210:     """Draws a traditional compass needle as a two-color diamond.
2211: 
2212: Diamond geometry in local coordinates, with the long axis along +x:
2213:     vertex 0 (+half, 0)      -> north tip, positive pole
2214:     vertex 1 (0, +half_w)    -> upper width
2215:     vertex 2 (-half, 0)      -> south tip, negative pole
2216:     vertex 3 (0, -half_w)    -> lower width
2217: 
2218: The diamond is split into two halves at the center (x, y):
2219:     north, white : triangle [0, 1, center, 3]
2220:     south, blue  : triangle [2, 1, center, 3]
2221: 
2222: After construction in local coordinates, rotation by theta and translation to (x, y) are applied.
2223: 
2224: Parameters
2225: ----------
2226: ax      : matplotlib axis on which to draw
2227: x, y    : needle center or pivot position
2228: theta   : needle angle [rad]
2229: length  : needle length
2230: width   : needle width"""
2231:     half   = length / 2.0
2232:     half_w = width  / 2.0
2233: 
2234:     # vertices in coordeanythings locais (not rotacionados)
2235:     pts_local = np.array([
2236:         [ half,     0.0    ],   # 0: tip north
2237:         [ 0.0,      half_w ],   # 1: width upper
2238:         [-half,     0.0    ],   # 2: tip south
2239:         [ 0.0,     -half_w ],   # 3: width lower
2240:     ])
2241: 
2242:     # matriz of rotation 2×2 pelo angle theta
2243:     c, s = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)
2244:     R = np.array([[c, -s],
2245:                   [s,  c]])
2246:     # applies rotation and translation
2247:     pts = (R @ pts_local.T).T + np.array([x, y])
2248: 
2249:     # north half: polygon [north_tip, upper_width, center, lower_width]
2250:     north = plt.Polygon(
2251:         [pts[0], pts[1], [x, y], pts[3]],
2252:         closed=True, facecolor=color_n,
2253:         edgecolor=edge, linewidth=0.5, zorder=zorder)
2254: 
2255:     # south half: polygon [south_tip, upper_width, center, lower_width]
2256:     south = plt.Polygon(
2257:         [pts[2], pts[1], [x, y], pts[3]],
2258:         closed=True, facecolor=color_s,
2259:         edgecolor=edge, linewidth=0.5, zorder=zorder)
2260: 
2261:     ax.add_patch(south)
2262:     ax.add_patch(north)
2263: 
2264:     # pino central (axis of rotation)
2265:     ax.plot(x, y, 'o', ms=2.0, color='#555555',
2266:             markeredgecolor='#222222', markeredgewidth=0.4,
2267:             zorder=zorder + 1)
2268:

2270: def draw_compass_batch(ax, xs, ys, thetas, length=0.42, width=0.10,
2271:                        color_n='#FFFFFF', color_s='#2E6DB4',
2272:                        edge='#1a1a1a', zorder=4):
2273:     """Vectorized version of draw_compass(): draws all needles in the lattice at once using two PatchCollection objects for the north and south halves and a single ax.scatter() call for the central pivots, instead of one ax.add_patch()/ax.plot() call per needle.
2274: 
2275: Performance motivation
2276: ----------------------
2277: Each individual ax.add_patch() triggers _update_patch_limits(), which traverses the path geometry, including Bezier curves, to update the axis bounding box. This fixed per-object cost becomes the dominant bottleneck when generating each frame with thousands of needles, measured around 1.5-1.85 ms per needle. PatchCollection receives all polygons at once and updates limits in batch, eliminating the repeated cost. The visual result is essentially identical, but rendering is much faster."""
2278:     half   = length / 2.0
2279:     half_w = width  / 2.0
2280:     x_flat = np.asarray(xs).ravel()
2281:     y_flat = np.asarray(ys).ravel()
2282:     th_flat = np.asarray(thetas).ravel()
2283:     K = x_flat.shape[0]
2284: 
2285:     # vertices locais (not rotacionados), same for all the needles
2286:     pts_local = np.array([
2287:         [ half,     0.0    ],   # 0: tip north
2288:         [ 0.0,      half_w ],   # 1: width upper
2289:         [-half,     0.0    ],   # 2: tip south
2290:         [ 0.0,     -half_w ],   # 3: width lower
2291:     ])   # shape (4, 2)
2292: 
2293:     # matrizes of rotation for all the K needles of a time: shape (K, 2, 2)
2294:     c = np.cos(th_flat)
2295:     s = np.sin(th_flat)
2296:     R = np.empty((K, 2, 2))
2297:     R[:, 0, 0] = c
2298:     R[:, 0, 1] = -s
2299:     R[:, 1, 0] = s
2300:     R[:, 1, 1] = c
2301: 
2302:     # applies the rotation of each needle to all four local vertices at once:
2303:     # pts_rot[k, v, :] = R[k] @ pts_local[v]   →  shape (K, 4, 2)
2304:     pts_rot = np.einsum('kab,vb->kva', R, pts_local)
2305:     # translada each needle for sua position (x_k, y_k)
2306:     pts_rot[:, :, 0] += x_flat[:, None]
2307:     pts_rot[:, :, 1] += y_flat[:, None]
2308: 
2309:     # builds the north/south polygons of each needle from the vertices already
2310:     # rotated and translated (same topology as the original version):
2311:     #   north = [ponta_norte, largura_sup, center, largura_inf]
2312:     #   south   = [ponta_sul,   largura_sup, center, largura_inf]
2313:     centers = np.stack([x_flat, y_flat], axis=1)   # shape (K, 2)
2314: 
2315:     north_patches = []
2316:     south_patches = []
2317:     for k in range(K):
2318:         p0, p1, p2, p3 = pts_rot[k]   # ponta_n, larg_sup, ponta_s, larg_inf
2319:         ctr = centers[k]
2320:         north_patches.append(mpatches.Polygon(
2321:             [p0, p1, ctr, p3], closed=True))
2322:         south_patches.append(mpatches.Polygon(
2323:             [p2, p1, ctr, p3], closed=True))
2324: 
2325:     pc_north = PatchCollection(
2326:         north_patches, facecolor=color_n, edgecolor=edge,
2327:         linewidths=0.5, zorder=zorder)
2328:     pc_south = PatchCollection(
2329:         south_patches, facecolor=color_s, edgecolor=edge,
2330:         linewidths=0.5, zorder=zorder)
2331:     ax.add_collection(pc_south)
2332:     ax.add_collection(pc_north)
2333: 
2334:     # central pins: a single scatter call for all needles, instead of
2335:     # K individual calls to ax.plot()
2336:     scatter_pins = ax.scatter(
2337:         x_flat, y_flat, s=4.0, c='#555555',
2338:         edgecolors='#222222', linewidths=0.4,
2339:         zorder=zorder + 1)
2340: 
2341:     return pc_north, pc_south, scatter_pins
2342:

2348: def _fmt_B(B):
2349:     """Formats field intensity in a readable unit: T, mT, or microtesla."""
2350:     if B == 0:      return "0 T"
2351:     if B >= 0.1:    return f"{B:.4f} T"
2352:     if B >= 1e-4:   return f"{B*1e3:.4f} mT"
2353:     return              f"{B*1e6:.2f} µT"

2356: def draw_ext_field_on_lattice(ax, xs, ys, B_ext, phi_ext_deg,
2357:                               needle_len, B_ext_max=None, B_signed=None,
2358:                               color='#FFD700'):
2359:     """Represents the external field in the image. It is always drawn, even when B_ext = 0, for example after a pulse has been turned off.
2360: 
2361: Elements
2362: --------
2363: 1. ARROWS AT SITES: golden arrows at each needle pointing in the field direction. When B_ext = 0, the arrows become invisible (alpha=0) but the reference panel remains visible.
2364: 
2365: 2. FIELD PANEL: box in the upper-right corner, mirroring the stopwatch geometry in the upper-left corner and avoiding overlap with the needles. It contains the current SI intensity and angle in degrees, a horizontal intensity bar, and a small direction arrow to the right of the bar. When B_ext = 0, the arrow is hidden, the text reads "0 T", and the bar is empty.
2366: 
2367: Parameters
2368: ----------
2369: ax           : matplotlib axis
2370: xs, ys       : needle positions
2371: B_ext        : external-field magnitude [T]
2372: phi_ext_deg  : external-field direction [degrees]
2373: needle_len   : reference needle length for scaling"""
2374:     phi      = np.deg2rad(phi_ext_deg)
2375:     cos_phi  = np.cos(phi)
2376:     sin_phi  = np.sin(phi)
2377:     B_max_ref = B_ext_max if (B_ext_max and B_ext_max > 0) else max(B_ext, 1e-30)
2378:     frac      = min(abs(B_ext) / B_max_ref, 1.0)   # 0→1, proportion of the maximum field
2379:     field_on  = (B_ext > 1e-30)                     # True if the field is nonzero
2380: 
2381:     # ── 2. panel field (ALWAYS visible) — corner upper right ──────
2382:     # Mirrors the clock geometry (upper-left corner): box
2383:     # retangular ancorada ao top, text and bar horizontal insidela.
2384:     # This avoids overlap with the needles, which remain in the central area.
2385:     xlim  = ax.get_xlim()
2386:     ylim  = ax.get_ylim()
2387:     xspan = xlim[1] - xlim[0]
2388:     yspan = ylim[1] - ylim[0]
2389: 
2390:     bar_w = 0.20 * xspan
2391:     bar_h = 0.018 * yspan

"""
============================================================
compass_simV48.py — Simulation of a compass-needle lattice V48
============================================================

Models a 2D grid of classical magnetic dipoles, represented as compass
needles, that interact through the magnetic field each needle produces at
its neighbors. The dynamics are inertial, using Newton's second law for
rotation with no pivot friction and viscous air damping. The integrator is
Velocity-Verlet. All physical quantities use SI units.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
COMMAND-LINE PARAMETERS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

┌─ LATTICE GEOMETRY ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                            │
│  --geometry  square | triangular | honeycomb               │
│              Lattice type. Default: square                 │
│              · square     : rectangular grid               │
│              · triangular : equilateral triangular grid    │
│              · honeycomb  : honeycomb, with hexagonal holes│
│                                                            │
│  --N         int   Number of needle ROWS. Default: 8       │
│  --M         int   Number of needle COLUMNS. Default: 8    │
│                                                            │
│  --R         float Radius of each needle circle [m].       │
│                    Neighbor distance = 2R.                 │
│                    Default: 0.025 m (2.5 cm)               │
│                                                            │
│  --needle_frac float Needle length as a fraction of        │
│                    the diameter 2R (0.0-1.0).              │
│                    Default: 0.80 -> needle = 80% of 2R     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─ PHYSICS AND SIMULATION ───────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                            │
│  --moment    float Magnetic moment of each needle [A·m²]   │
│                    Default: 0.1 (table compass, about 5 cm)│
│                    Ref: pocket ≈ 0.01 | nautical ≈ 1.0     │
│                                                            │
│  --inertia   float Moment of inertia [kg·m²]. If omitted,  │
│                    it is computed automatically from the   │
│                    geometry: steel sheet using R,          │
│                    needle_frac, --needle_thickness,        │
│                    and --steel_density.                    │
│                                                            │
│  --damping   float Viscous air damping [N·m·s/rad]         │
│                    Controls the quality factor Q:          │
│                    Q = omega_0·I/b (high Q = more          │
│                    oscillatory motion). Default: 5e-8      │
│                    (Q≈25, realistic compass). For a smooth │
│                    B_ext=0.1 T run, use 8e-6 (Q≈4).        │
│                                                            │
│  --t_sim     float Total physical simulation time [s].     │
│                    Sum of all integrated dt steps,         │
│                    equivalent to what a real stopwatch     │
│                    would measure while observing the       │
│                    moving needles. The video displays this │
│                    physical time. The simulation stops     │
│                    earlier if S=1.00 or at rest.           │
│                    Default: 2.0 s                          │
│                                                            │
│  --dt_factor float Fraction of the natural period T0 used  │
│                    as the integration step (0.02-0.10).    │
│                    Smaller = more accurate, slower.        │
│                    Default: 0.05                           │
│                                                            │
│  --noise     float Initial-noise amplitude [rad].          │
│                    0 = all needles point toward +x         │
│                    pi ≈ 3.14 = fully random orientation    │
│                    Default: 1.5                            │
│                                                            │
│  --seed      int   Random-number-generator seed.           │
│                    Ensures reproducibility.                │
│                    Default: 42                             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─ UNIFORM EXTERNAL FIELD (SI units) ────────────────────────┐
│  Two ways to specify the field. Do not use both together.  │
│                                                            │
│  Form A — magnitude + angle, recommended:                  │
│  --B_ext     float Field magnitude [T].                    │
│                    0.0      = no field (default)           │
│                    50e-6    = Earth's field (≈50 µT)       │
│                    1e-3     = fridge magnet at 5 cm        │
│                    0.1      = strong field (aligns all)    │
│                                                            │
│  --phi_ext   float Field direction [degrees].              │
│                    0   = right (+x), default               │
│                    90  = up (+y)                           │
│                    180 = left (-x)                         │
│                    270 = down (-y)                         │
│                    Counterclockwise sense. Default: 0.0    │
│                                                            │
│  --ext_Bx    float x component of the field [T]            │
│  --ext_By    float y component of the field [T]            │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─ OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PNG files are always generated in the current directory:  │
│    compass_initial.png      initial state                  │
│    compass_equilibrium.png  final state                    │
│    compass_comparison.png   side-by-side comparison        │
│    compass_order_param.png  order parameter S(t)           │
│                                                            │
│  --video     str   Path of the MP4 video to generate.      │
│                    Requires ffmpeg. If the file already    │
│                    exists, saves as name0001.mp4,          │
│                    name0002.mp4, etc.                      │
│                    Example: --video simulation.mp4         │
│                                                            │
│  --frame_every int Save one frame every N steps.           │
│                    Smaller = smoother video, slower run.   │
│                    Default: 5                              │
│                                                            │
│  --fps       int   Frames per second of the MP4 video.     │
│                    Default: 24                             │
│                                                            │
│  --keep_frames     If present, keeps the folder of         │
│                    intermediate PNG frames after MP4       │
│                    generation.                             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─ CONTROLS DURING THE SIMULATION ───────────────────────────┐
│  The simulation stops automatically when:                  │
│    · S = 1.00, all needles aligned                         │
│    · The lattice is at rest, omega_max -> 0                │
│    · The requested t_sim time is reached                   │
│    · Ctrl+I (Tab) is pressed in the terminal               │
│      -> interrupts and saves the video immediately         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

# ── GPU acceleration backend (optional) ──────────────────────────────────
# If the package 'cupy' is installed AND an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) estiver
# available, uses CuPy as a NumPy replacement for heavy computations
# (dipolar field). CuPy has an API that is almost identical to NumPy, so the same
# vectorized code runs on the GPU without logic changes.
# If cupy is not installed, there is no GPU, or the CUDA headers
# Toolkit are not present (needed to compile kernels in
# runtime), automatically falls back to NumPy (CPU) — the programa
# works on any machine, even with cupy "partially" installed.
_GPU_AVAILABLE = False
_GPU_ERROR_MSG = None
_xp = np   # _xp = "array module" active: np (CPU) or cp (GPU)
try:
    import cupy as cp
    # Test 1: is there the visible CUDA device?
    cp.cuda.Device(0).compute_capability
    # Test 2 (critical): actually tries to COMPILE and execute the simple kernel.
    # cp.cuda.Device(0).compute_capability only queries the driver — does not detect
    # missing headers of the CUDA Toolkit, which are required for the NVRTC
    # compilar kernels elementwise (cos, sin, etc.) in runtime.
    # Without this real test, the error only appears in the middle of the simulation.
    _test_arr = cp.array([0.0, 1.0])
    _ = cp.cos(_test_arr)   # forces JIT compilation of the real kernel
    cp.cuda.Stream.null.synchronize()
    _xp = cp
    _GPU_AVAILABLE = True
except Exception as _e:
    _xp = np
    _GPU_AVAILABLE = False
    _GPU_ERROR_MSG = str(_e).strip().splitlines()[-1] if str(_e).strip() else type(_e).__name__


def _to_cpu(arr):
    """Converts an array from the active backend, GPU or CPU, to a plain NumPy array."""
    if _GPU_AVAILABLE and hasattr(arr, 'get'):
        return arr.get()
    return arr


def _to_backend(arr):
    """Converts a NumPy array to the active backend, GPU or CPU."""
    if _GPU_AVAILABLE:
        return cp.asarray(arr)
    return np.asarray(arr)


# ── configure output for immediate flushing and correct line endings ──────────────
# On macOS with zsh, keyboard raw mode (used by Ctrl+I) may disable
# the processing of \n → \r\n in the terminal. Forcing line_buffering and flush
# ensures that each print() appears correctly on its own line.
sys.stdout.reconfigure(line_buffering=True)

def _print(*args, **kwargs):
    """Replacement for print() that guarantees immediate flushing and correct CRLF line endings, even when the terminal is in raw mode, as on macOS/zsh with Ctrl+I enabled."""
    import sys
    msg = ' '.join(str(a) for a in args)
    sys.stdout.write(msg + '\r\n')
    sys.stdout.flush()


def _progress_ansi_ok():
    """Returns True if stdout is an interactive terminal (TTY). This enables the live two-line panel using ANSI codes. For redirected output, such as logs or pipes, it returns False and the code uses the legacy behavior without escape codes that would pollute the file."""
    import sys
    if _PROGRESS_REGION['ansi'] is None:
        try:
            _PROGRESS_REGION['ansi'] = bool(sys.stdout.isatty())
        except Exception:
            _PROGRESS_REGION['ansi'] = False
    return _PROGRESS_REGION['ansi']


# state of the live progress-bar panel (V44):
#   'open' : True while the two lines (bar + status) are on the screen
#   'ansi' : TTY detection cache (None = not yet checked)
_PROGRESS_REGION = {'open': False, 'ansi': None}


def _print_progress_bar(frac, prefix="", suffix="", status_line=None,
                        bar_width=40):
    """Prints or updates the progress panel (V44): two live lines rewritten in place at each update.

Example:
    Integrating [CPU] [########            ]  42.3%  step 970/2294
    [step 970/2294]  t=2.4310s  B=+0.0000mT  S=0.4415  w_max=3.1rad/s

In an interactive terminal (TTY), ANSI codes move the cursor and clear lines so the two lines are redrawn in place instead of accumulating new lines. For redirected output (non-TTY), the function uses the legacy behavior: the bar is updated with '\r' on a single line, and the caller prints status as normal log lines.

Parameters
----------
frac        : completed fraction, between 0.0 and 1.0
prefix      : text before the bar, e.g. "Integrating [CPU] "
suffix      : text after the percentage, e.g. "step 524/1007"
status_line : second panel line, or None
bar_width   : number of characters in the bar itself

Note: any normal _print() message emitted while the panel is open should come after _print_progress_bar_finish(), which moves the cursor below the panel and marks it as closed."""
    import sys
    frac = max(0.0, min(1.0, frac))
    n_filled = int(round(frac * bar_width))
    bar = '#' * n_filled + ' ' * (bar_width - n_filled)
    pct = frac * 100.0
    bar_line = f"{prefix}[{bar}] {pct:5.1f}%  {suffix}"

    if _progress_ansi_ok():
        status = status_line if status_line is not None else ""
        # Protocol with cursor invariant (V44): at the END of each drawing,
        # the cursor remains parked at COLUMN 0 OF THE BAR LINE (top of the
        # panel). Each update then redraws downward:
        #   clear line (\x1b[K) + bar + moves down ("\n\r", robust with or
        #   without translation ONLCR by the terminal driver) + clears + status +
        #   moves up (\x1b[1THE) + returns to column 0 (\r).
        # This is independent of the position where the text ends (without depending
        # on \n returning to column 0, which varies between terminals/ptys) and
        # works at the bottom of the screen (the "\n" causes the required scroll).
        seq = ("\x1b[K" + bar_line + "\n\r" +
               "\x1b[K" + status + "\x1b[1A\r")
        sys.stdout.write(seq)
        sys.stdout.flush()
        _PROGRESS_REGION['open'] = True
    else:
        # legacy (not-TTY): bar overwriting its own line via \r
        sys.stdout.write("\r" + bar_line)
        sys.stdout.flush()


def _print_progress_bar_finish():
    """Closes the progress panel: moves the cursor to a new clean line below the panel, keeps the final two lines visible, and marks the panel as closed. In ANSI mode it is safe to call this when the panel is already closed, because it emits nothing and avoids spurious blank lines."""
    import sys
    if _progress_ansi_ok():
        if _PROGRESS_REGION['open']:
            # cursor is at column 0 of the bar line: move down two lines
            # (bar -> status -> new line below the panel)
            sys.stdout.write('\n\r\n\r')
            sys.stdout.flush()
            _PROGRESS_REGION['open'] = False
    else:
        sys.stdout.write('\r\n')
        sys.stdout.flush()

# 1. PHYSICAL CONSTANTS (International System — SI)
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# μ₀/(4π) = 1×10⁻⁷  T·m/A  (vacuum permeability / 4π)
MU0_OVER_4PI = 1.0e-7   # T·m/A

# ── Default physical parameters of a table compass needle (~5 cm) ──────
#
# Magnetic moment
#   moment = 0.1 A.m2 (typical diamond-shaped sheet needle)
MOMENT_DEFAULT = 0.1      # A·m²   (typical table compass needle)
#
# Needle mass and geometry (thin steel bar, length L, circular cross section)
#   mass   m ≈ 0.5 g  = 5×10⁻⁴ kg
#   length L ≈ 5 cm = 0.05 m
#   Moment of inertia of thin bar about its center:
#       I = (1/12) · m · L²  =  (1/12) · 5×10⁻⁴ · (0.05)²  ≈ 1.04×10⁻⁷  kg·m²
INERTIA_DEFAULT = 1.0e-7  # kg·m²

# Density of common magnetic steel (carbon steel / silicon steel for use
# electromagnetic, the used in transformer laminations or compasss
# of mesa). Typically ranges between 7700-7900 kg/m³; we use the value
# representative of the ordinary carbon steel.
STEEL_DENSITY_DEFAULT = 7850.0   # kg/m³
# Default thickness of a thin sheet cut from ordinary steel sheet
NEEDLE_THICKNESS_DEFAULT = 0.4e-3   # m  (0.4 mm)

# Saturation magnetization of a common magnetic steel (carbon steel / ferro
# doce). Corresponds to a saturatestion flux density Bsat ≈ 2.0 T,
# well-established value in the literature for iron alloys of alta
# permeability (typical range: 1.6-2.2 T; we use the value central
# representative). Relation: Bsat = μ0 · Ms  →  Ms = Bsat / mu0.
STEEL_MS_SATURATION_DEFAULT = 1.59e6   # A/m  (≈ Bsat of 2.0 T)


def compute_inertia_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness,
                                  density=STEEL_DENSITY_DEFAULT):
    """Computes the moment of inertia of a needle modeled as a thin, homogeneous rectangular sheet rotating about the axis perpendicular to the sheet plane and passing through the center of mass. This is the z axis and represents the real rotation axis of a compass needle supported by a pivot.

Physical model
--------------
Rectangular sheet with length L, width w, thickness t, mass m, and density rho:

    m = rho · L · w · t                         [kg]

Moment of inertia of a thin rectangular plate about the axis perpendicular to its plane through the center:

    I = (1/12) · m · (L² + w²)                  [kg·m²]

This formula generalizes the thin-bar case, I = mL²/12, valid when w -> 0. Here the w² term is kept explicitly because real needles cut from sheet metal have non-negligible width. The thickness t enters only through the mass. A thin sheet has a negligible intrinsic inertia term in the direction perpendicular to its plane, m·t²/12, when t << L,w.

Parameters
----------
needle_len   : needle length L [m]
needle_width : needle width w [m]
thickness    : sheet thickness t [m]
density      : material density [kg/m³], default: common magnetic steel, 7850 kg/m³

Returns
-------
I : moment of inertia [kg·m²]"""
    mass = density * needle_len * needle_width * thickness   # [kg]
    I = (1.0 / 12.0) * mass * (needle_len**2 + needle_width**2)   # [kg·m²]
    return I


def compute_moment_from_geometry(needle_len, needle_width, thickness,
                                 Ms=STEEL_MS_SATURATION_DEFAULT):
    """Computes the magnetic moment of a needle modeled as a thin rectangular sheet of magnetic steel, saturated along its long axis, the north direction of the needle. In other words, the whole needle is assumed to be magnetized up to the material's physical limit, with all magnetic domains aligned along its length.

Physical model
--------------
For a saturated ferromagnetic material, the total magnetic moment is the product of saturation magnetization Ms and volume V:

    m = Ms · V                                  [A·m²]
    V = L · w · t                               [m³]

This is the same rectangular-sheet geometry L×w×t used in the inertia calculation. Here the full needle volume is assumed to contribute to magnetization, an ideal case of uniform saturation. Real needles may have magnetization slightly below the theoretical saturation because of shape demagnetization, but full saturation is the physical upper limit and a reasonable reference for a well-magnetized needle.

Parameters
----------
needle_len   : needle length L [m]
needle_width : needle width w [m]
thickness    : sheet thickness t [m]
Ms           : material saturation magnetization [A/m], default: common magnetic steel, about 1.59e6 A/m, corresponding to Bsat ≈ 2.0 T

Returns
-------
m : magnetic moment [A·m²]"""
    volume = needle_len * needle_width * thickness   # [m³]
    m = Ms * volume                                   # [A·m²]
    return m

#
# Viscous damping (air resistance to needle rotation).
# The effective Q depends of the dominant field B_eff = max(B_dipolar, B_externo):
#   Q = omega_0·I/b   where  omega_0 = sqrt(m·B_eff/I)
#
# With B_ext = 0.1 T:   omega_0 ≈ 316 rad/s  →  b = 8e-6 gives Q ≈ 4  (smooth)
# With B_ext = 0  :     omega_0 ≈  13 rad/s  →  b = 5e-8 gives Q ≈ 25 (compass)
#
# The default 5e-8 is suitable for simulating with no external field or weak field.
# For strong fields (> 1 mT), use --damping 1e-6 or 1e-5 for smooth motion.
DAMPING_DEFAULT = 5.0e-8  # N·m·s/rad

# 2. MAGNETIC DIPOLAR FIELD (SI)
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def dipole_field_2d(rx, ry, theta_src, moment):
    """Computes the magnetic field produced by a dipole in the XY plane, using SI units.

Exact 3D magnetic-dipole field, evaluated in the z=0 plane:

    B = (mu0/4pi) · [ 3(m_hat·r_hat)r_hat - m_hat ] / r³

In Cartesian components, with m = moment·(cos theta, sin theta, 0):

    Bx = (mu0/4pi) · [ 3(m·r)·rx / r⁵ - mx / r³ ]
    By = (mu0/4pi) · [ 3(m·r)·ry / r⁵ - my / r³ ]

SI units:
    moment [A·m²]
    rx, ry [m]
    Bx, By [T]

Parameters
----------
rx, ry    : components of r = receiver point - source dipole [m]
theta_src : angle of the source dipole relative to the +x axis [rad]
moment    : magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment of the source needle [A·m²]

Returns
-------
(Bx, By) : magnetic-field components at (rx, ry) [T]"""
    r2 = rx**2 + ry**2
    if r2 < 1e-24:
        # avoids division by zero when the point coincides with the source
        return 0.0, 0.0

    r  = np.sqrt(r2)          # distance  [m]
    r5 = r2 * r2 * r          # r⁵  [m⁵]

    mx = moment * np.cos(theta_src)   # x component of the moment  [A·m²]
    my = moment * np.sin(theta_src)   # y component of the moment  [A·m²]

    mdotr = mx * rx + my * ry         # m · r  [A·m³]

    Bx = MU0_OVER_4PI * (3.0 * mdotr * rx / r5  -  mx / (r2 * r))
    By = MU0_OVER_4PI * (3.0 * mdotr * ry / r5  -  my / (r2 * r))
    return Bx, By   # [T]


# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# 3. TOTAL FIELD ON THE NEEDLE (SI)
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def total_field_on(i, j, thetas, xs, ys, cutoff, moment,
                   pbc=False, Lx=None, Ly=None, n_images=1):
    """Sums the dipolar field from all neighboring needles onto needle (i, j).

For computational efficiency, only needles within the cutoff radius are considered. This is physically justified because the dipolar field decays as 1/r³, so distant contributions are negligible.

Periodic boundary conditions (PBC)
----------------------------------
When pbc=True, the lattice is treated as a unit cell repeated infinitely in x and y, creating a periodic structure without edges. For each needle pair (i,j)-(ni,nj), the field is summed over all periodic replicas within ±n_images cells in x and y, not only the nearest image. With n_images=1, the default, each neighbor contributes through (2·1+1)² = 9 replicas: the original cell plus one replica on each side in x and y, equivalent to the classical minimum-image convention. Increasing n_images includes more distant replicas and is useful when the cutoff is large relative to the lattice period.

This removes edge effects: needles at the boundary see neighbors from the opposite side, and their more distant replicas, as if the structure were infinite.

Parameters
----------
i, j     : indices of the receiver needle in the N×M grid
thetas   : 2D array with current angles of all needles [rad]
xs, ys   : 2D arrays with fixed needle positions [m]
cutoff   : maximum interaction radius [m]
moment   : magnetic moment of each needle [A·m²]
pbc      : if True, applies periodic boundary conditions [bool]
Lx, Ly   : lattice periods in x and y [m], required only when pbc=True and computed in make_grid
n_images : number of periodic replicas to sum on each side in each direction, default 1. Total replicas considered per neighbor = (2·n_images+1)² cells.

Returns
-------
(Bx_tot, By_tot) : total field at needle (i, j) [T]"""
    Bx_tot, By_tot = 0.0, 0.0
    N, M = thetas.shape
    xi, yi = xs[i, j], ys[i, j]

    # periodic replica shifts to consider (0 = original cell)
    if pbc and Lx and Ly:
        img_range = range(-n_images, n_images + 1)
        x_shifts = [k * Lx for k in img_range]
        y_shifts = [k * Ly for k in img_range]
    else:
        x_shifts = [0.0]
        y_shifts = [0.0]

    for ni in range(N):
        for nj in range(M):
            if ni == i and nj == j and not pbc:
                continue  # without PBC: the needle does not interact with itself

            rx0 = xi - xs[ni, nj]   # [m]
            ry0 = yi - ys[ni, nj]   # [m]

            for dx_img in x_shifts:
                for dy_img in y_shifts:
                    # skips the needle itself in the original cell (zero distance)
                    if ni == i and nj == j and dx_img == 0.0 and dy_img == 0.0:
                        continue

                    rx = rx0 + dx_img
                    ry = ry0 + dy_img
                    dist = np.sqrt(rx*rx + ry*ry)

                    if dist > cutoff:
                        continue  # outside the cutoff radius: ignore

                    bx, by = dipole_field_2d(rx, ry, thetas[ni, nj], moment)
                    Bx_tot += bx
                    By_tot += by

    return Bx_tot, By_tot   # [T]

def _plot_hysteresis(log, hyst_autoscale=False):
    """Plots the hysteresis curve M_proj(B) and saves it as PNG and CSV.

The plot shows the magnetization projected along the field direction as a function of the applied-field magnitude, the classical M-H hysteresis curve.

Parameters
----------
log : list of tuples (t, B_scalar, M_proj, S), generated during integration with field_mode='hysteresis'
hyst_autoscale : bool, default False. If True, autoscales the axes of the hysteresis curve. """
    log = np.array(log)
    t_arr  = log[:, 0]
    B_arr  = log[:, 1] * 1e3    # converts T → mT for readability
    M_arr  = log[:, 2]          # projected magnetization (dimensionless, ∈ [−1,1])

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5), facecolor='#1A1A2E')

    # ── left panel: M×B (hysteresis curve) ─────────────────────────
    ax1 = axes[0]
    ax1.set_facecolor('#0D1B2A')
    ax1.plot(B_arr, M_arr, color='#E94560', lw=1.2, alpha=0.85)
    ax1.axhline(0, color='#4A4A6A', lw=0.6, ls='--')
    ax1.axvline(0, color='#4A4A6A', lw=0.6, ls='--')
    ax1.set_xlabel("Campo B  [mT]",    color='#BDC3C7')
    ax1.set_ylabel("Magnetização  M (projeção)",  color='#BDC3C7')
    ax1.set_title("Curva de Histerese  M × B", color='#ECF0F1',
                  fontfamily='monospace')
    ax1.tick_params(colors='#7F8C8D')
    ax1.grid(True, color='#2C3E50', alpha=0.5)
    for sp in ax1.spines.values():
        sp.set_edgecolor('#2C3E50')

    if not hyst_autoscale:
        B_max = np.max(np.abs(B_arr))
        if B_max < 1e-5:
            B_max = 1.0
        ax1.set_xlim(-1.05 * B_max, 1.05 * B_max)
        ax1.set_ylim(-1.15, 1.15)

    # ── right panel: M(t) and B(t) versus time ──────────────────────────
    ax2 = axes[1]
    ax2.set_facecolor('#0D1B2A')
    l1, = ax2.plot(t_arr, M_arr, color='#E94560', lw=1.2, label='M (proj.)')
    ax2b = ax2.twinx()
    ax2b.plot(t_arr, B_arr, color='#FFD700', lw=1.0, alpha=0.7,
              ls='--', label='B (mT)')
    ax2b.set_ylabel("Campo B  [mT]", color='#FFD700')
    ax2b.tick_params(colors='#FFD700')
    ax2.set_xlabel("Tempo físico  t  [s]", color='#BDC3C7')
    ax2.set_ylabel("Magnetização  M", color='#E94560')
    ax2.set_title("Evolução temporal", color='#ECF0F1', fontfamily='monospace')
    ax2.tick_params(colors='#7F8C8D')
    ax2.grid(True, color='#2C3E50', alpha=0.4)
    for sp in ax2.spines.values():
        sp.set_edgecolor('#2C3E50')
    lines = [l1, plt.Line2D([0],[0], color='#FFD700', ls='--')]
    ax2.legend(lines, ['M (proj.)', 'B (mT)'], facecolor='#1A1A2E',
               edgecolor='#2C3E50', labelcolor='#ECF0F1', fontsize=8)

    fig.suptitle("Simulação de Histerese Magnética — Rede de Bússolas",
                 color='#BDC3C7', fontsize=12, fontfamily='monospace')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("hysteresis_loop.png", dpi=130, bbox_inches='tight',
                facecolor='#1A1A2E')
    plt.close(fig)
    _print("  Gráfico de histerese salvo: hysteresis_loop.png")


def _plot_sine(log, freq):
    """Plots M(t) and B(t) for the sinusoidal-field mode and saves the result as PNG.

Parameters
----------
log  : list of tuples (t, B_scalar, M_proj, S)

    log   = np.array(log)
    t_arr = log[:, 0]
